back: The Group I elements (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, francium). They react with water to form alkaline hydroxide solutions.

front: Why are lithium, sodium and potassium stored under oil?
back: They react quickly with oxygen and water vapour in the air; the oil keeps the air away.

front: Give four physical properties of lithium, sodium and potassium.
back: Soft (cut with a knife); shiny when freshly cut but tarnish quickly; low density (they float on water); low melting points for metals.
Melting point decreases; density increases (generally); reactivity increases.
notes: Potassium is an exception to the density trend: it is less dense than sodium.

front: General equation for a Group I metal M reacting with water
notes: The hydroxide makes the solution alkaline.

front: What is seen when lithium is added to water?
back: It floats and fizzes steadily, moving slowly around the surface until it disappears. It does not melt.

front: What is seen when sodium is added to water?
back: It floats, melts into a shiny ball, fizzes rapidly and darts around the surface until it disappears.

front: What is seen when potassium is added to water?
back: It floats, melts and fizzes violently; the hydrogen catches fire with a lilac flame; it may spit and crackle.

front: Why does reactivity increase down Group I?
back: The single outer electron is further from the nucleus in each element down the group, so it is less strongly attracted and lost more easily.

front: Predict how rubidium and caesium react with water.
back: Even more violently than potassium (explosively), forming a hydroxide (RbOH, CsOH) and hydrogen.
notes: They also have lower melting points than potassium.
